title: Circadian modulation of dopamine release shapes reward-evoked signaling in the nucleus accumbens
content:
Abstract
The circadian system is an important regulator of reward-related neural function and behavior. Dopamine (DA) release in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) is a key component of reward processing, yet how circadian timing shapes DA release in relation to reward behavior remains unclear. Here, we investigated circadian rhythms in DA release and reward behavior in C57BL/6J mice expressing the genetically encoded DA sensor DA3m in the NAc using long-term fiber photometry paired with an automated reward delivery and measurement system. Spontaneous DA, reflecting broad changes in DA release during natural behavior, peaked during the early subjective day. In a separate group of mice, targeted disruption of the molecular clock gene Bmal1 in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) strongly attenuated spontaneous DA rhythmicity, supporting a role for the SCN molecular clock in regulating these rhythms. Reward-evoked DA peaked during the day-to-night transition, while cue-evoked DA and reward behavior peaked during the early subjective night. Linear mixed-effects modeling showed that reward-evoked DA was positively associated with reward behavior and cue-evoked DA but negatively associated with baseline DA measured immediately before reward availability. Reward-evoked DA differed across circadian time even after accounting for reward behavior or cue-evoked DA, while higher baseline DA predicted smaller reward-evoked responses and the strength of this relationship also changed across circadian time. Together, these findings show that circadian time changes both the magnitude of reward-evoked DA responses and how those responses relate to baseline and cue-evoked dopamine signaling and reward behavior.
